prompt.context: Our client, Shermer Pharma, is a venture-backed start-up pharmaceutical company. Over the past 15 years, Shermer has been developing a molecule that has been approved by the FDA to cure Alzheimer's with 90% efficacy.
prompt.question: Shermer's owners have hired us to answer two questions: (1) How should we sell our product? (2) Is our product going to be profitable?

clarifying_info.a: It is a pill that cures Alzheimer's — an illness that currently has no treatment that cures or stops the progress of the disease.

clarifying_info.q: How large is the Alzheimer's market?
clarifying_info.a: 30 million people suffer worldwide. (Let the candidate size the market first; then provide the actual addressable market figure of 5 million users.)
Sales would be focused on neurologists and geriatric psychiatrists, not directly to the consumer.

clarifying_info.q: Does Shermer have a sales or marketing organization today?
clarifying_info.a: No. The company has purely been a research firm to this point and has no Sales or Marketing organization.

clarifying_info.q: Has the product received regulatory approval?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. FDA approval has been granted.
Shermer is the only firm with a cure for this illness and will be for the next 5 years. We will not focus on competitive response during this case.
R&D costs total $1.5 billion. The firm requires that R&D costs be recovered by Year 5 of the product.

clarifying_info.q: What is the gross margin per user?
clarifying_info.a: Annual gross margin per user is $1,000. Manufacturing and packaging costs are included in this gross margin figure.
G&A costs are $25 million per year.

clarifying_info.q: Should we account for taxes or NPV?
clarifying_info.a: We can ignore taxes and NPV for this analysis; assume straight-line amortization of R&D over 5 years.

exhibits.title: Sales Force Options
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of two sales force options — Develop Own Sales Force vs. Contract Sales Force — with several cells left blank for the candidate to calculate.

exhibits.title: Annual Net Income
exhibits.shows: A 5-year P&L table with projected market penetration rates given and all financial rows (Total Users, Total Gross Margin, Amortized R&D Costs, Selling Costs, G&A Costs, Net Income) left blank for the candidate to complete.

data.All other rows: blank — candidate must calculate using data provided through clarifying questions

framework: Market entry approach: Identify and evaluate the three options for building a sales and marketing capability — (1) develop own internal sales force, (2) use a contract sales organization, (3) sell Shermer to a larger firm with existing commercial capabilities.

Financial analysis: Size the Alzheimer's market, estimate market penetration over 5 years, build a P&L (gross margin minus amortized R&D, selling costs, and G&A) to determine if and when the product becomes profitable.
Sales force cost comparison: Calculate the total annual selling cost under each viable option using Exhibit 1, identifying which channel is cheaper.
Profitability check: Complete the Exhibit 2 P&L table across Years 1–5 to confirm the product recovers R&D costs and turns profitable before the 5-year competitive window closes.
Recommendation: Synthesize the qualitative (core competency, organizational readiness) and quantitative (cost, profitability) findings into a clear recommendation.

questions.prompt: What are the three options for going to market, and what are the key trade-offs of each?
questions.guidance: Strong answer covers: (1) Build own sales force — full control, 100% focus, but high upfront cost and requires building a new organizational capability from scratch, which is outside Shermer's R&D-focused core competency. (2) Contract sales organization — lower cost, faster to stand up, but reps only devote 50% of their time to Shermer's product (split attention). (3) Sell the company to a larger pharma firm — optimal if owners are open to it; the acquirer has all commercial infrastructure already; candidate should raise this proactively even though no financial data is provided for it.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the missing values: cost per sales call for own sales force, total calls required for contract sales, total sales reps needed for contract sales, and total annual selling cost for both options.
questions.guidance: Candidate should walk through the math systematically. Own sales force cost per call = $200k × 85 calls per rep / 1000 calls per rep (i.e., each rep makes 1,000 calls/year at $200k salary) — the casebook derives $170 as ($200k × 85) / 100k. Contract needs 2× the calls because reps are only 50% focused. Total reps for contract = 85 × 2 = 170. Total annual cost comparison reveals contract is cheaper: $12MM vs $17MM.

math.setup: Own sales force: 85 reps × $200k fully loaded cost = total cost. Derive cost per call = ($200k × 85) / 100k total calls. Contract: 100k calls required × 2 (because 50% focus) = 200k calls; at $60/call = total cost.
steps: Own — cost per sales call: ($200k × 85 reps) / 100k calls = $17MM / 100k = $170 per call
Own — total annual selling cost: 85 reps × $200k = $17MM
Contract — total calls required: 100k × 2 = 200k (due to 50% focus)
Contract — total annual selling cost: 200k calls × $60 = $12MM
math.answer: Own sales force total annual selling cost = $17MM; Contract sales force total annual selling cost = $12MM. Contract sales is cheaper by $5MM per year.

questions.prompt: Size the Alzheimer's market. How many patients might be addressable in the US or globally?
questions.guidance: Let the candidate attempt the sizing (e.g., estimate US population, age distribution, prevalence rate). A reasonable approach: ~330M US population, ~15% over 65, ~10–15% of those with Alzheimer's ≈ 5–7M. After the exercise, provide the correct figure of 5 million total addressable users.

math.setup: Estimation exercise. Interviewer provides the answer of 5MM after candidate attempts.
steps: Candidate estimates using population pyramids or prevalence rates
Interviewer confirms: Total addressable market = 5 million patients

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2 and the data provided, complete the 5-year P&L. Calculate Total Users, Total Gross Margin, Amortized R&D Costs, Selling Costs, G&A Costs, and Net Income for each year. Does the product recover R&D costs by Year 5?
questions.guidance: Candidate must apply: Total Users = penetration rate × 5MM; Gross Margin = Total Users × $1,000/user/year; Amortized R&D = $1.5B / 5 = $300MM/year; Selling Costs = $12MM/year (contract); G&A = $25MM/year; Net Income = Gross Margin − $300MM − $12MM − $25MM. Year 1 will be negative; by Year 2 it turns positive; by Year 5 cumulative profits far exceed R&D investment.

math.setup: Total Users = market penetration % × 5,000,000. Gross Margin = Total Users × $1,000. Net Income = Gross Margin − $300MM (R&D amortization) − $12MM (selling costs) − $25MM (G&A).
steps: Year 1: Users = 5% × 5M = 250k; Gross Margin = 250k × $1,000 = $250MM; Net Income = $250MM − $300MM − $12MM − $25MM = −$87MM
Year 2: Users = 10% × 5M = 500k; Gross Margin = $500MM; Net Income = $500MM − $300MM − $12MM − $25MM = $163MM
Year 3: Users = 25% × 5M = 1.25MM; Gross Margin = $1.25B; Net Income = $1.25B − $337MM = $913MM
Year 4: Users = 40% × 5M = 2MM; Gross Margin = $2B; Net Income = $2B − $337MM = $1.663B
Year 5: Users = 60% × 5M = 3MM; Gross Margin = $3B; Net Income = $3B − $337MM = $2.663B
math.answer: Year 1 Net Income = −$87MM (loss). Product turns profitable in Year 2 ($163MM). By Year 5, annual Net Income = $2.663B. R&D costs are fully amortized within the 5-year window.

brainstorming.prompt: Before engaging the go-to-market plan, what additional factors should Shermer consider?

categories.name: Sales force effectiveness
ideas: Contract sales reps split attention 50/50 — lower effectiveness per call compared to dedicated reps
For an incremental $5MM/year, Shermer could build its own sales force and gain full dedication — qualitatively defensible even if financially suboptimal at low revenue years
Dedicated reps may build deeper relationships with neurologists and geriatric psychiatrists

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: $1,000/year for a life-saving, first-in-class cure for an incurable disease is significantly underpriced
Pricing could be revised substantially upward given the disease burden, zero competition for 5 years, and willingness-to-pay of patients and payers
Reimbursement strategy with insurers and Medicare/Medicaid is critical

categories.name: Organizational and strategic options
ideas: Selling Shermer to a larger pharma firm may be optimal — acquirer brings ready-made commercial infrastructure, regulatory affairs, distribution, and payer relations
Licensing the molecule is another asset-light monetization path
Partnering for co-promotion with a firm that already calls on neurologists is a hybrid option

categories.name: Market and patient access
ideas: Diagnosis rate for Alzheimer's — not all patients are formally diagnosed or under neurologist care
Caregiver and family decision-making role in treatment adoption
Patient assistance programs and payer coverage negotiations

categories.name: Risks
ideas: Generic / biosimilar entry after patent expiration beyond Year 5
Manufacturing scale-up risk as volume grows from 250k to 3MM users
Adverse event or safety signal post-launch could trigger recalls or label changes
Reputational risk if pricing becomes a public controversy

recommendation: Shermer Pharma should go to market via a contract sales organization targeting neurologists and geriatric psychiatrists, which costs $12MM per year versus $17MM for an in-house force — saving $5MM annually while leveraging Shermer's existing R&D focus.

The product will be profitable: while Year 1 produces a −$87MM loss due to R&D amortization, the business turns profitable in Year 2 and generates $2.663B in net income by Year 5, fully recovering the $1.5B R&D investment well within the 5-year exclusivity window.

Ideally, Shermer should explore selling the company to a larger pharma firm with established commercial capabilities, which may represent the highest-value exit for venture backers and eliminate execution risk in an unfamiliar function.
risks: Contract sales force is less effective per call (50% focus) — real sales conversion may underperform the model
$1,000/year price point appears significantly underpriced; upside exists but so does payer negotiation risk if repriced
Year 1 cash flow is negative ($87MM loss); Shermer needs bridge financing or venture runway
No prior commercial experience creates organizational execution risk regardless of channel chosen
next_steps: Negotiate and finalize contract sales organization terms, including minimum call frequencies and rep training on Alzheimer's
Conduct a formal pricing analysis comparing willingness-to-pay, payer reimbursement benchmarks, and competitor precedents for first-in-class CNS drugs
Explore M&A / licensing conversations with top-10 pharma firms with neurology franchises
Build out G&A infrastructure (medical affairs, regulatory, market access) needed to support launch
